For explorations, surveys, mapping and investigations; for publication of English and French editions of reports, maps, illustrations, etc., relating thereto; and for salaries and wages of explorers, topographers and others, $366,000.

Could the minister give
particulars of the increase in this vote?

speakeroldname: Hon. T. A. CRERAR (Minister of Mines and Resources):
speechtext:
The amount of $366,000 is
broken down into two parts, one covering explorations, surveys, mapping, investigations and salaries and wages of those engaged in the work, which totals $258,600, and the other covering the publication of English and French editions of reports, maps and illustrations which are put out once the field notes of the survey parties are coordinated and extended.

Is the increase of $16,000
for the extension of this work?

I think that is made up
mainly of statutory increases for those in the permanent service.
What work was carried on in British Columbia last season?
There were nine geological and six topographical parties in British Columbia last year.

There was some work
being carried on in the vicinity of Vancouver and on the lower mainland; has that been completed?

This work is never really
completed. A party will work in a certain area and the work for that area will be completed once the notes are extended and the maps and other information based on the data gathered in the field put together, but when work is completed in one area there is generally another area where it must be continued.

That is just the point I was trying to make. This work was started in the district around Mission City and it will take at least another season to complete the work through to Hope. There was some doubt whether this work would be completed under the topographical survey vote. The district in question is very important in lumbering, logging and mining, and we are anxious to have this work completed.

A couple of years ago this parliament voted a million dollars for exploration work in the mining areas of Canada. Could the minister tell the committee how much of that was spent and for what purpose?
That was the vote passed in 1935?
Yes.
I have not the information at the moment as to how much of that was spent.
Was it not spent mostly in 1936?
I am advised that the greater part was spent in the summer and autumn of 1935. We had another vote last year for $350,000.
That was a revote to complete the work, was it not?
No, that was for new work. This is really an extension of the same work.
I am unable to give my right hon. friend the information as to how much of that million dollar vote remained unexpended at the end of 1935.
At March 31, 1936.
At the end of the period.

How was this vote of $350,000 spent last year, and was it really a continuation of the work started in 1935?
Sup-ply-Mines and Resources

There were nine geological and six topographical parties in British Columbia; there were two geological parties in the Northwest Territories; there were four geological parties in Alberta; there were five in Saskatchewan, one being engaged in Ottawa in compiling data obtained the previous year; there were five geological parties in Manitoba and five in Ontario; there were five geological and two topographical parties in Quebec; there were four geological parties in New Brunswick; there were three geological parties in Nova Scotia and one topographical party. In all, there were forty-five geological and nine topographical parties, one geological party being engaged in Ottawa.
Does the minister consider that the information obtained by these parties justified the expense?

I have no hesitation in saying that I think the expense is justified. By the terms under which Manitoba and British Columbia came into confederation we have to maintain a geological service for those two provinces. As far as Quebec and Ontario are concerned, both provinces send out parties under their own mines branches. This work is carried on in cooperation with the mines branch at Ottawa in order to avoid duplication.
What about the Northwest Territories?
We had two parties operating there last year. Of course, this work is entirely under federal government supervision.
Is there any topographical work being carried on there?
My deputy advises me that there will be no aerial work carried on under this vote. Some aerial photographic work was carried on under the old department of the interior.
I asked a question a few moments ago as to whether this geological work would be continued.
Where are the four geological surveys operating in Alberta?

I might mention as an illustration of the value of the work done by these parties the circumstances that led to the development of the radium industry in the Northwest Territories. In 1900 the first geological party that ever went into the Great Bear lake area prepared a report upon their explorations, and that report lay in the archives of the department at Ottawa for

almost thirty years, until a prospector who was perusing the report was struck with a single sentence in it to the effect that there was evidence of cobalt blue on the shores of Great Bear lake. That led to his making an expedition to Great Bear lake, and carrying on an investigation into the extent of the cobalt mineral, and while doing so he discovered pitchblende ores which had escaped the observation of the geological party thirty years before. That was the beginning of the radium industry in Canada, developed as a result of these explorations of the Great Bear lake area. I mention that as an evidence of the value of gathering this field data, which is available to prospectors who wish to take advantage of it.
In reply to my hon. friend who asked as to parties operating in Alberta, one party was operating in the Edmonton and Peace Hills field, another in the Pekisko area, and two parties in southeastern Alberta, the latter two parties studying the geology more from the point of view of petroleum.

I think last year there was a topographical survey party with headquarters at Mission City on the lower mainland of British Columbia. I understand that another season will complete their work. Can the minister give me any encouragement that the work will be continued?
That is now under consideration. The officials of the department are now mapping out the season's work, and I am advised that work will probably be continued in that area this year.
Would the minister tell the committee just in what way and by what methods the personnel of these parties throughout the country is selected?

The parties are headed by experienced geologists, as many as possible from the department itself. We also secure for chiefs of the parties some help from outside, in some cases professors of geology or mining at some of the universities. Then we endeavour to secure university students who are taking courses in geology or mining engineering, preferably third or fourth year students, because they are interested in the work and it has a direct bearing on the calling which they have selected for themselves in life. The ordinary help is secured in the usual way in the localities where the parties are working.

I hope the ordinary help is not selected in the same way that the ordinary help for the Post Office Department is selected. Can the minister assure us that

Supply-Mines and Resources
he uses a different and a fairer method than the Post Office Department follows in engaging temporary help for the Christmas rush?

I should have to consult my colleague the Postmaster General to discover the method by which he selects his help. But I assure my hon. friend that we endeavour to get the help locally as far as possible, and I do not think there can be much criticism of the department in that regard.

I should like to say for
the information of the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) that I submitted twenty-six names and got only one appointment, and the appointee was in his final year at engineering.
I submitted many names and got no appointment.
As money is going to be spent for exploration purposes, would the minister tell us if by any chance any money is going to be spent for work on roads leading to mines? Would that be under this item?
No.
Under what item would it come?
Under an item in the special supplementary estimates when they are brought down.
I understood the minister to say that four survey parties were operating in Saskatchewan. May I ask in what part of Saskatchewan?
There were four parties in Alberta and five in Saskatchewan.
I understood the minister to say that four parties were operating in Saskatchewan and that one party was in Ottawa tabulating the material. Is that correct?

That is correct. There was one party operating in the Fort Pitt area; another at Forster lake in the northern part of the province; another party in southwestern Saskatchewan, studying underground water resources, and another party in southwestern Saskatchewan at Riverhurst, carrying on exploratory work in oil surveys. There was a large party at Goldfields to investigate gold occurrences in that district.
Could the minister tell the committee what are the prospects of a profitable development of the magnetic iron ore of British Columbia at Texada island and other points in the province?

I am afraid I cannot give my hon. friend very much information on that point, having nothing about it at the moment. I understand that they are not producing, but that it is a fairly good grade of ore.
Has any investigation been made of the deposits on Texada island? They are located at tidewater, with lime and everything else that is necessary, and with coal not far distant.
Reports have been published on these ores that my hon. friend speaks of, but I have not seen them myself and consequently I cannot speak with any knowledge.
Are the reports of these survey parties immediately available, and, if so, where can they be had?

They can be secured from the director of mines and geology. Of course, it takes a little time to put all the data into the form of a report. The field parties make their observations, and after they return from the field the report is compiled. As soon as available it is printed and ready for distribution. If my hon. friend has in mind some particular reports and will make inquiry of the director of mines and geology he can readily ascertain whether or not they are available at the present time.
Would the minister tell us something about the portion of the item that refers to forest products laboratories?
We shall come to that a little later. The item which we are now considering does not relate to that.

On the border line between Saskatchewan and Manitoba is the extensive Flin Flon development, and on the western border between Saskatchewan and Alberta are the Goldfields deposits. It is estimated that there are some 8,000 square miles of the Cambrian shield in, the northern part of Saskatchewan. That is a most interesting formation, and it occurs to me that if an extensive survey were made this year or in succeeding years there might be some important developments in that area. I should like to know what is the intention of the department as regards survey work in the northern part of Saskatchewan.

Tentatively the department has had under consideration the sending of another party into the Goldfields area, that is in the lake Athabaska region, and also in what is known as the Cree lake area, which is, I am told, south and east of lake Athabaska.
Sup-ply-Mines and Resources

Whether it touches the particular area to which the hon member has alluded I do not know; I am informed that it does.

Item agreed to.
For maintenance of offices and museum; for purchase of instruments, chemicals, books of reference, museum equipment and specimens, and related supplies; for expenses of the Geographic Board of Canada; and for miscellaneous assistance and contingencies, $74,000.

Will the
minister give us a breakdown of that item of expense for maintenance of offices and museum, -purchase of instruments, e-t cetera?

It includes the maintenance of offices, the maintenance of the museum, the purchase of instruments, chemicals for the mineralogical work and the assaying and the like; books of reference; miscellaneous assistance and contingencies; and the expenses of the Geographic Board of Canada, which has to do with the designation of geographical names. That takes up practically the whole vote. Then there is a small item of 83,000 for museum equipment, and another small item of $1,000 for the purchase of specimens for the museum. That side of the museum work has been left somewhat in the -background owing to the necessity of curtailing expenditures as much as possible.
The annual report of the Department of Mines, March 1936, states that the work of the national museum is retarded by overcrowding.
I think probably that is correct.
Are there any proposals for the remedying of this condition?

I am informed that there has been some rearrangement of the office space, and that the difficulty alluded to in the report has been thereby overcome. We are endeavouring to operate as economically as possible. I think that in some cases our staffs are working under overcrowded conditions, but we are doing the best we can.

Item agreed to.
Miscellaneous-
To provide for payments in connection with the movements of coal under conditions prescribed by the governor in council and for the cost of administration thereof, $2,25-0,000.

Would the minister be good enough to make a clear and comprehensive statement as to this expenditure, showing where the subventions last year went, the extent of them, and what subventions it is 
proposed to continue? I indicated the other day that I had a communication-in fact I have had several communications-in connection with the matter. There is grave anxiety in the west in connection with the subventions, and likewise there is anxiety regarding portions of the subventions in eastern Canada, particularly with respect to the movement of Nova Scotia coal and the difficulties that have been experienced in connection therewith. Perhaps the hon. gentleman would make the matter clear.

There has been some
anxiety, I believe, about this question of coal subventions. It is not intended to make any change this year in the principle upon which subventions are based. That principle is that the subvention applies to put the Canadian producer in as good a position as the American producer, in certain areas and in certain markets. Obviously if the cost of producing American coal increases and the cost of producing Canadian coal remains stationary, under the operation of the order in council upon which the subventions are based the total amount paid would be reduced. Conversely, if the cost of Canadian coal advances and American coal costs remain stationary, the subventions would increase. Last year there was a slight reduction in certain cases in the actual cash per ton paid by way of subvention. That was due to the fact that American costs had increased, consequently it did not require the same amount to bring about the equalization upon which the order in council applying the subventions is based. When we come to the amount of subventions paid, we did not provide enough money last year. It appeared to be enough in the light of the experience of the previous year, but the expansion in business and the increased shipments of coal left us short in our provision.
Would the minister state the amount of subventions paid and to whom they were paid, commencing say in western Canada?

I find that in the calendar year 1936 the amounts in round numbers were as follows:
Nova Scotia	$1,573,000
New Brunswick	 15,000
Alberta	 307,000
Alberta-Ontario movement.. 163,000
Saskatchewan	 38,000
British Columbia	 113,000
It is paid partly to the railways. I have not the details here, if my right hon. friend means the actual recipients.

Supply-Mines and Resources

I know that the railways received some, of course, but I should like to have on Hansard a record of the persons or corporations to whom the subventions were paid, and the amounts for the calendar year. The minister can obviously see the reason. The auditor general's report for the year 1936 will not be available until next year, so that this is the only opportunity to secure the information. I can readily understand that the minister has not the information at the moment. We can either let the item stand, or he can give the information later. There are some further questions I desire to ask with respect to subventions, particularly with respect to some of the western subventions and the apprehension some have as to the possible curtailment of them. I was going to predicate my questions upon the answers given to the question I have just asked.

I think I can have the
information available after the six o'clock recess. Meantime we might continue discussion of the item and then let it stand until after recess.

I should like to know
the quantities of coal moved as a result of these subventions.

Nova Scotia coal moved,
1.681.000	tons.
To Ontario?

It would be to Quebec
and Ontario. For instance, a considerable quantity moved to Noranda, I think some
225.000	to 250,000 tons. Then a very considerable amount was moved to the International Nickel Company at Sudbury. In New Brunswick the total tonnage on which the subvention applied was 20,953 tons; in Alberta and British Columbia, the Crowsnest area, 298,000 tons; Alberta-Ontario movement, 65,229 tons.

Perhaps the minister
would make clear how that Alberta-Ontario item is split up. Part of it moved to what I would call the Toronto urban area, and I think it moved as far east as Ignace. It will be remembered that there was provision for the movement as far east as Ignace. I should like to know to what extent it came east to Winnipeg on the main lines, so to speak, and the diversion down to the urban centres of Ontario.
The figure I have just given, 65,229 tons, is the domestic coal movement to Ontario. The other movement to which my right hon. friend refers is probably in connection with the railway requirements.
Steam coal.
Yes. I shall endeavour to get the information on both.

A considerable volumr of Nova Scotia coal is imported into Ontario. I use some myself in some of my buildings. The board of education in Toronto uses a lot of it. I wonder what will be the effect on Ontario importations of Nova Scotia coal of the proposed importation of Russian coal. If there is any effect from the proposed importation of 250,000 tons a year will the minister require the additional $300,000 that he asks for in the estimates? Because if Ontario and Quebec are to use 250,000 tons of Russian coal that will mean 250,000 tons less of Nova Scotia coal.
I do not think it will have the effect my hon. friend mentions.
The Russian coal has to be sold somewhere, and the price would not permit of its being sold in Nova Scotia.
The Nova Scotia coal is steam coal. The Russian coal, if any, that will be imported under the arrangement, is anthracite. They do not compete with each other.

Can the minister give the amount of coal produced in Nova Scotia prior to the granting of the subsidies and the amount produced since the subsidies have been in effect? I should like to find out what effect the subsidies have had in increasing the production of coal in Nova Scotia.
I have not that information here. How far back does my hon. friend wish to go?
Not very far back; just prior to the time the subsidy was granted. What amount of coal has been produced in Nova Scotia since the subsidy has been in effect?
Subventions have been in effect, as I recall it, for some eleven or twelve years.

I was wondering whether the subventions have had any appreciable effect in increasing production in Nova Scotia. If they have not, I do not see the use of continuing them. If they have had some effect, their continuance might be worth while.

There is another angle to that question which perhaps my hon. friend has overlooked, and it is this. Of recent years, say within the last ten years, fuel oil has to a considerable extent displaced coal for the heating of dwellings and also to a certain



Supply-Mines and Resources
extent in providing power for driving ships and so on. So if my hon. friend were to base his judgment on a comparison of the coal production in Nova Scotia say twelve or fifteen years ago with the present coal production under the subventions, he would need to take into account several other factors as well.

That is true, but there was quite a bit of oil in use prior to the establishment of the subventions, and I should think that would be taken into consideration. What I wished to find out was whether these subventions have had the effect originally intended.

Inasmuch as at least a large portion of the subvention has been paid during the five years from 1930 to 1935 I think I should say to the hon. gentleman (Mr. Heaps) that but for the subventions the mines of Nova Scotia would have been practically shut up. The reason is obvious. It is not a question of fuel oil alone, as the minister has said. There was another question, that of the prices at which coal was being thrown upon Canadian markets from the United States, and other countries as well. It was impossible, even with the tariff increases that were put in effect, for the coal from Nova Scotia to compete with the fuel that came from Virginia, for instance. All hon. members who are familiar with the cost at which fuel from that locality was being offered for sale to upper Canadian factories will realize the situation, and the subventions barely made it possible under the conditions that then existed for those mines to supply the steam coal requirements of upper Canadian factories.
On Friday last I was talking to a manufacturer who had continued to use Nova Scotia coal. He told me that the pressure to utilize other fuels imported from outside Canada had been very great, but under the circumstances he felt that the action taken by the country was right; he was endeavouring to do what he could to assist, and he gave his reasons, which struck me as being eminently sound. I think I can say without fear of successful contradiction, however, that but for these subventions the island of Cape Breton would have been in a very serious condition indeed. Since it did not result in any political advantage to the particular government that happened to be in power during those years I can speak of it with much more certainty than perhaps I otherwise could. That this is a fact can be amply demonstrated by anyone who cares to take the trouble to look into the matter.
As far as the west is concerned I can only say that but for the subventions the coal
[Mr. Crerar.)
would not have moved at all east of, we will say, Swift Current. In Winnipeg they have had a terrific struggle to establish any market for their coal as against coal coming there from the United States. The increase in duty that we imposed upon certain types of United States coal had some effect in decreasing the amount of coal that was imported. Last year substantial quantities of German coal came into this country, and in one or two instances I am afraid it came in under the name of Welsh coal. That, however, is not the type of coal with which we are now dealing, as the minister said a moment ago. We are dealing not with coal of the anthracite type but with bituminous coal. It will be remembered that the United States passed a statute by which they provided that there should be a duty against our lignite if under our tariff we imposed a duty against their lignite, and we did put them on the free list, as will be recalled. There was some very small movement of lignite from what you might call the southern Alberta fields into the states contiguous to Canada, directly south, and, as the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) is aware, there was some movement of coal from Great Britain and other quarters to Vancouver which seriously affected the position of the coal industry of Vancouver island, about which he used to speak so feelingly. I suppose now, under brighter skies and in different days, there is less necessity for the hon. member to direct attention to those hardships. The unwillingness of the hon. gentleman to participate in most debates that involve any reflection upon the present administration would indicate that the skies are much brighter even than I thought. Perhaps this may have the desired effect of getting the hon. member for Comox-Alberni to his feet so that we may hear from him.

Mr. Speaker, there is another side to this question, and it is a very tender point to the people at the head of the lakes. This coal subvention constitutes a protection to western coal and a duty on United States coal, and it has resulted in considerable unemployment at the head of the lakes. We have two large coal handling plants there; the machinery in one of those plants costs about three and a half million dollars. As the right hon. leader of the opposition has said, we are under brighter skies now, and I had hoped that these subventions would be very materially decreased and that the coal coming into Fort William might go a considerable distance further west, though perhaps not as far as Winnipeg. Our boats carry wheat east, and formerly they would bring back coal, so that these subventions

Supply-Mines and Resources
hit the shipping on the great lakes. We hope the day will come when there will be a considerable improvement in the amount of coal handled at the head of the lakes.

Despite the unkind remarks of the right hon. leader of the opposition I will give him credit for having been at the head of the government which first started the bonusing of coal on Vancouver island. I recall very clearly that after the election of 1930 a delegation waited upon the right hon. gentleman, who was then prime minister. That delegation consisted of a man from Nanaimo, a man from Cumberland-who was my late opponent, by the way-and myself. The other two members of the delegation were pressing the prime minister to impose a duty on fuel oil. The right hon. gentleman asked my opinion and I said I did not think that would be effective. I thought the better and more practical way would be to bonus the production of coal on Vancouver island, and my right hon. friend was pleased to say that he agreed with me. That was the procedure finally adopted, and a bonus of only twenty-five cents per ton was provided. Later on it was increased, but it all occurred while his government was in power, and I think if the other parties to the deal had played the game the result would have been very marked. At any rate I am quite free to say that his was the first and only government that did give us a bonus, and the benefits which resulted certainly were substantial.
And look what happened to him.

Possibly I was more concerned with what would happen to the hon. member for Comox-Alberni than with what might happen to the right hon. leader of the opposition.
I should like to ask the minister for certain information. Some of it he may be able to give me now, and if he has not the rest of it perhaps he will get it while he is getting the other information that has been requested. He has stated that the subvention to British Columbia for the calendar year 1936 amounted to $113,000. I should like to know how much of that amount was paid for coal produced on Vancouver island. I should like to know also how much of that was paid at the rate of fifty cents per ton and how much was paid at the other rate of a dollar a ton, because there are the two rates. Then I should like to ask the minister if there is any danger of an alteration, or any proposal to alter these rates of bonus during the ensuing year.
With regard to the amount mentioned by my hon. friend, that was all paid on Vancouver island.
And how much was paid at the fifty cent rate?
At the moment I cannot answer that.
The information could be obtained?
I dare say it could be secured.
Is there any proposal to change that bonus during the coming year?
No; that has not been under consideration so far.
And to whom was it paid?

We will secure that information also.
I might say a word in reply to what was said by the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Heaps) a moment ago. In the calendar year 1932 the total production of coal in Nova Scotia amounted to a little more than
4,000,000 tons, and the amount of subvention paid in that year was $710,000. Whether or not it was due to the subvention-and I assume it was an important factor-in 1936 there was an increase to over 6,500,000 tons. Unquestionably the payment of the subvention did have a definite bearing upon the total quantity of coal produced in Nova Scotia.
May we have similar figures for Alberta?

In 1931 the output in Alberta was 4,500,000 net tons, while in 1936 it exceeded 5,600,000 tons. In 1931 the total amount moved to Ontario was 23,400 tons and in 1936 it was slightly in excess of 65,000. In 1931 the subvention for the movement to Ontario was $127,000 and in 1936, $163,000.

It would be extremely difficult to get much information from the figures submitted, other than that between 1931 and 1936 there was an increase. There probably would have been an increase anyway, because 1936 was a better trading year than 1931.
Yes; quite true.

I do not know by what
means we may estimate the beneficial effects of subventions to Alberta and Nova Scotia. Naturally I am anxious to see the coal mining industry in Canada in a prosperous condition. I know how bad it was back in 1930, and in years prior to that. I remember having been sent to Alberta about nineteen years ago to make an investigation in the coal mining industry, and at that time very little Alberta coal was being used in Manitoba. I remember that the Alberta coal pro-

Supply-Mines and Resources
duoers got busy in an effort to capture the Manitoba market, and they succeeded fairly 'well, without any subvention. As the minister must know, to-day the consumption of Alberta coal in Manitoba is very great; it has almost entirely supplanted the American anthracite formerly used in Manitoba for domestic purposes. I do not see why something along the same line could not be done without these large subventions. True, we have tried to bonus Alberta coal coming into Ontario, but I believe without much success. Had the effort been successful the amount of coal moved would no doubt have been considerably greater.
A few minutes ago the question was raised as to the comparative costs of coal in Canada and in the United States. I am always puzzled as to why the cost of production in the United States is so much less than it is in Canada. In these observations I am not referring to any particular mine or area, but am speaking in a general way. I know there are some mines in Nova Scotia which are expensive indeed to operate-I refer to the mines running under the sea, where costs of operation are extremely high-but there are other mines in that province and throughout Canada where the cost of production should not be any higher than it is in some of the United States mines. Yet one finds that the cost of coal at the mine mouth in Canada is probably fifty per cent higher than it is across the boundary line, and I cannot understand why the difference should be so great. Wages cannot be responsible for it, because the wage rate in the United States is just as high as it is in Canada. I wonder if the minister has any information he can give the committee showing comparative costs of producing coal in various mines of the United States and Canada, because after all if the subvention is based upon the difference in cost of production in the two countries, the first thing the department should find is the comparative cost. Only thus can we gain any intelligent idea as to why subventions must be granted to the coal mining industry in Canada.

I think the fuel board have in considerable detail the information to which the hon. member refers. In order to apply the subventions in accordance with the principle of law governing them, that information must be available. Of course the cost of production varies in different mines in Alberta, Saskatchewan and Nova Scotia. This is an exceedingly difficult piece of legislation to administer to the satisfaction of all. In the operation of the subvention we must be guided

by the principle involved when subventions were originally granted, and apply it in the most intelligent manner. So far as my knowledge goes, and I am sure in this connection I speak correctly, it is applied without any discrimination.
Broadly I believe the rate is about one-seventh of a cent per ton per mile; am I correct?
Is that the basis on Vancouver island?
No, that is an export basis.
I am informed that in Saskatchewan and Alberta it works out to a ten per cent reduction in the freight rate.
I thought the largest subvention, payable from the maritimes to Ontario, was one-seventh of a cent per ton per mile. I may be wrong, because I am speaking from memory.
I would not be certain of the amount, but I believe payment is based on that principle.
Arising out of what the minister has just stated to the committee, may I ask if it is the policy of the government to grant the same subvention to different mines in the same province?
I did not catch my hon. friend's question.
Would there be any difference in the subventions paid to the different mines in Nova Scotia?
Yes, there is.
Is the hon. member referring to Nova Scotia mines only?
I was taking them as an example.

The amount of the subvention paid will vary with the cost of getting the coal into a particular market. For instance, the subvention on New Brunswick coal will be less than it is on Nova Scotia coal because Nova Scotia coal is further from the market.

Let me give an illustration. There are two mines in New Brunswick; in one costs of production are low while in the other they are high. Both mines want to send coal into Montreal. Would the subventions paid to each mine be the same?

If they were shipping by water, yes; if they were both shipping by rail, the subventions would be the same.

Supply-Mines and Resources
It would appear that costs of production are not a factor.

It is not a case of cost of production in two mines which may be located alongside each other in the same province; it is cost of production in the province as against cost of United States coal that would apply.
Is it not more the fact that the coal is entering a competitive market? It is possible that coal could go into Montreal without being paid a subvention.

I remember protesting some years ago against certain subventions which were being suggested at that time. They were referred to as experimental rates to enable Alberta coal to be brought into Ontario; the idea was to bring coal through provinces where the temperature goes to forty below to a province where it rarely goes below twenty above. I should like to know if in the payment of subventions we have reached the point where coal from one end of the country under subventions is meeting coal from the other end of the country under subventions, the two coals fighting for the same market. If we have not come to that point yet, I fear we shall reach it some day.
Not yet but soon.

I should like to find out something about this British Columbia subvention. What is the idea of paying a subvention on coal on Vancouver island when the boats call in there for bunkers? What is the basis of that subvention and is there any sense to it at all?
In so far as it was initiated by the last government, it is without sense; in so far as it has been continued by the present government, it is highly commendable.
I would not say that; I would say it is without sense in connection with both governments.
The real basis is the high cost of production on Vancouver island. Perhaps the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) could debate this matter better than I.

Naturally we are anxious to get a Canadian market for Canadian coal. Alberta produces large quantities of coal and it would seem that the metal mining districts in northern Manitoba and Saskatchewan would be logical markets for Alberta coal. Has the minister any information as to where the Hudson Bay Mining and Smelting Company at Flinflon get their supplies of coal?
I understand they purchase their coal in Alberta, but I am not certain just where in the province.

Do I understand the minister to say that there will be a reduction of about ten per cent, and that that will be based upon mileage as well as upon costs of production? How will that affect shipments of Alberta coal to the east?
I did not say that.
Is it to be only on a production basis, with mileage not entering into the matter at all?

I am informed it amounts to ten per cent. Obviously, if you are hauling your coal a thousand miles, you will be paying more freight per ton than if you are hauling it only five hundred miles, but the ten per cent would apply in both cases.

I should like to say a
word in support of these subventions. I made a special trip to Sydney, Nova Scotia, to ascertain just what these subventions meant in the way of emploj^ment for the miners of that district. I was driven out to Glace Bay and Waterford. I asked one of the principal mining men how much coal was being shipped to Ontario and how much employment was being provided through these subventions. We happened to be standing near the railway tracks and just then a train pulled by consisting of thirty-seven cars holding approximately 2,000 tons of coal. On the side of the train was a big poster stating, "Nova Scotia coal for Ontario." It must have taken quite a number of men to mine thirty-seven cars of coal. I asked this gentleman if they were sending out many trains like that one, and he told me that they were. If that train was only one of many, then these subventions must be providing considerable employment for Nova Scotia miners. As I said a moment ago, I have used Nova Scotia coal and I am highly in favour of bringing that coal into Ontario. We ship a considerable quantity of manufactured material to the eastern provinces and in my opinion it is good business to encourage interprovincial trade. I am convinced from what I saw at Glace Bay that the money provided for in this vote is money well spent for Canada.

There is just one thing
wrong with the payment of subventions on coal. The two central provinces benefit greatly from the protection about which the hon. member who just sat down always talks. When those two provinces want to buy coal, the hon. member becomes very solicitous for

Supply-Mines and Resources
the miner in Nova Scotia and he wants to have Nova Scotia coal brought into Ontario. He wants Ontario to buy Nova Scotia coal, and he wants somebody to pay part of the freight rate for bringing that coal into Ontario. It seems to me there is something wrong in trying to get it both ways. First, he wants protection on manufactured goods to help out his working men, and then he wants part of the freight paid on coal to help out the working men in the outermost provinces of the dominion. I would say this, that this thing of protection and this thing of subventions are the curse of this country, and the sooner we get rid of them and get relief in both ways, the better it will be for Canadians from coast to coast.

I should like to say a word on subventions. Those who come from Alberta or British Columbia or from the east realize fully that subventions are of great value. In the first place, to deal with what the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Young) has just said, if this coal is not protected and these subventions are not given, the money which Ontario would spend for coal would go to the United States, and that would be exceedingly poor business for Canada.
Why?

Moreover, the railroads of this country, which are already a serious anxiety to Canada, would lose that traffic. That again is a serious matter. In addition to this, we would be keeping in employment United States working men instead of Canadians in Alberta, British Columbia, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. After all is said and done, the only thing that makes this country valuable is the number of people who are living here and who can continue to make a living here. If we once make conditions such that they can no longer make a living here, then they are no longer able to buy goods, and the railroads will lose the traffic from carrying the goods to them. So, in the last analysis, while I do not wish to advocate anything which will bring about an altogether artificial condition, we must grant the fact that it is a sound principle to protect up to a certain point at least.
I come from Alberta, and I know how we look at the matter out there. The subventions have meant a great deal to us.
Sure.

There are some who are inclined to say "sure," but let them remember that Alberta is one of the nine provinces of this dominion, and if we destroy the

economic stability of any one province we seriously impair the economic condition of the whole country. Consequently, we must all be ready to give and take, to be open-minded in all these matters.
The coal subventions, let me tell the minister, have meant a great deal to Alberta, and I assume they have meant just as much to the other provinces. It is a matter of great satisfaction to us that these subventions have increased the amount of our trade, and I wish to commend them highly. I regret that the hon. member for Fort William1 (Mr. Mclvor), I think it was, had to report that there was a lack of employment at the head of the lakes because coal was no longer being brought in there from across the line. That is bad, but it goes to show how we can hardly help anyone without hurting somebody else. At the same time we must remember that when United States coal is coming in here, United States miners are mining that coal and United States railways are hauling it. So, on the whole, I think these subventions are to the advantage of the dominion even if it means that the men at the head of the lakes are hurt, as my hon. friend says; but we could probably find some way of compensating them. I would say to the minister that he is following a strictly sound policy when he furthers the application of these subventions; in fact, I would rather be inclined to think that if he increased them to some extent it would still be sound, so that we would not be on a strictly competitive basis with producers outside. After all, it does seem most unsound, when we have such a tremendous amount of coal in Alberta, and when that coal is of so many different kinds, that we should buy coal from across the line. So I do not hesitate for one minute to commend the minister for his activity in this respect, and to urge that he follow this plan in the future to a greater extent even than he has in the past.

I cannot let this opportunity pass without taking exception to the remarks of the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Young). He seems to be deeply concerned about the fact that subvention is paid for the benefit of our coal miners. You can call it a subvention or bonus or whatever you like, but if my hon. friend were to take the time to study the amount of bonuses and subventions that have been given to the wheat growers of Canada, he would find that the subvention on coal is very, very small in comparison. The eastern provinces, make no mistake, have paid their share, and paid through the nose for years, for the benefit of the farmers of the west. I do not like the

Supply-Mines and Resources
impression to go out through the country that we in the east are getting something that we do not deserve. The advantage which Canada derives from these subventions-and I say this fairly and honestly-cannot be gauged by the amount of the subvention paid, because it puts into the hands of the miners purchasing power which they otherwise would not have. Without the subvention we could not keep the markets we have. Competition has been so keen in the last number of years that our markets could not have been retained, let alone increased, without the subvention. I can speak for Nova Scotia, and for New Brunswick too, in this matter. They have furnished an excellent market for the wheat products of the western provinces and for their cattle in the shape of meats. There is no better market than our eastern provinces for the manufactured products of the central provinces, a statement which I am sure any manufacturer in Ontario or Quebec will corroborate. Our miners are doing arduous work, and they have to live on the very best food; their work demands it; otherwise they could not stand the strain of producing coal. When we take into consideration what our miners did in the war years, when their manpower was depleted, I think we should all resent a remark like that made by the hon. member for Saskatoon going on the Hansard of this dominion; and in saying that, I speak for the miners all over Canada.

I would say to my hon. friend that he can never embarrass me by talking about bonuses paid on wheat. I am not in favour of bonuses, no matter where they are applied, and I would like that to be very well understood. There was a wheat bonus duiing past years when the wheat industry was in danger perhaps of almost being wiped out, and the country came to its rescue under those circumstances. I take it that there will be no division of opinion as to the necessity for aid when such are the circumstances.
We supplied a board to sell your wheat too, and we bought your wheat.
Not very much. The hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) takes this attitude. He is strong for protection on goods manufactured in Ontario, and he pleads the cause of the working man.
I always will.

His desire to help the working man is no greater than that of any other hon. member. He wants to help the working man of Ontario. He also professes great concern about buying coal from Nova Scotia.
He is not suggesting that there be about $5 a ton duty against United States coal, and that the people of Ontario be made to pay whatever that protected cost of coal might be.
The duty is only 50 cents a ton.

That would be a different proposition altogether. The rest of the country would then have to pay the subventions, and that is not charged up to my friend when he burns his coal in Ontario.
Let me say to the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Hartigan) that if he will take the trouble to study the production of real wealth in the western provinces during the last twenty-five years, he will be amazed to learn the amount of real wealth that has come out of those provinces. Further, he might study the question of how much these same provinces paid the dominion as a result of burdensome tariffs, our own province alone being charged up with a bill of about $28,000,000 a year.
What about the rest of Canada?

The hon. member will then begin to realize what this burden means to those of us who live in that part of the country. We are not opposed to Nova Scotia miners selling all the coal they can. We have no objection to Alberta miners selling all the coal they can. But we ask that these things be done on a basis which does not require the rest of Canada to pay for it all the time. In Saskatchewan, which is an extremely cold province during the winter months, the only satisfaction we have had was an increase some time ago from $2.20 per ton to $2.80 per ton in freight rates out of the Alberta field. But there is no subvention for us; we have to pay the bill. I have paid so many coal bills that I know something about the subject of prices and freight rates. All we are suggesting is this, that this whole matter should be given full consideration and that unfair burdens should be lifted from the backs of those in western Canada who have been bearing these burdens for a very long time. The hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) rises in his place in the house to ask for subventions, and makes a great plea for what I call protection.
Protection for the Canadian worker.

The other day I read a speech in which the hon. member expressed himself as being very much in favour of the budget in that it represents a downward revision-not so much as some of us would like

Supply-Mines and Resources
but a revision in the right direction. Now, you cannot have it going and coming. There is a principle at stake here.
I am quite aware of that.

You must apply the same principle no matter whether it be for you or against you, if it is sound. We in Saskatchewan have no more desire to be unfair to our Alberta and Nova Scotia friends than, I am sure, they have any desire to be unfair to us. Let me point out that it is because of the most burdensome protection which has been imposed in the interests of eastern industries that both ends of Canada have suffered as greatly as they have for a long time.
May I ask the minister how much money by way of subventions on coal was granted to Saskatchewan last year?
I shall have the information in a few moments.

While the minister is getting the information, I should like to say that, like other western members who have spoken, I am in favour of as large a reduction as possible of a tariff which has worked in favour of the industrial part of central Canada. We in the west, like hon. members from the maritimes, have come to realize that we can go only a certain distance in the direction of free trade, that apparently we shall always have to submit to a certain measure of protection in this country. As I understand the matter, subventions on coal from Nova Scotia and Alberta are intended to make up in a small measure to those parts of Canada for what they are losing because of the tariff; in other words, it was recognized that those provinces gain practically nothing from the tariff, but lose a great deal, and these subventions are intended to provide some measure of compensation. My opinion is that so long as certain parts of Canada are to benefit at the expense of other parts through our fiscal tariff policy, until the benefits and injuries can be balanced to some extent by a substantial reduction, of the tariff, anything that helps those parts which are penalized should have my support. So far as Saskatchewan is concerned, may I say that we shall have to recognize the fact that other parts of Canada will demand and receive in the years to come a certain degree of protection.
On a point of order: We are not entitled to discuss the budget under this item. The tariff is not the subject before the committee at the moment; the subject is subventions on coal.
Apparently the tariff is before the committee.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I do not think the point of order of the hon. member for Davenport is well taken. Hon. members have been allowed a wide latitude.

I am surprised that the
hon. member for Davenport rose to that point of order-he of all members-
Will the hon. member explain why every western member considers himself qualified to ask questions and express views as to the sentiments of members from the maritime provinces?
Only Saskatchewan members.
I can answer that: because we suffer from the same fiscal policy that has almost ruined the west as well as the maritimes.
Let us speak for ourselves.

The only fiscal policy which will bring this country together is one that will deal fairly with all parts of the dominion. We have had a policy which has assisted the industrial part of central Canada at the expense of the maritimes and western Canada as well as at the expense of the agricultural part of central Canada; in other words, it has benefited only the industrial area of central Canada at the expense of other parts, and that to the tune of roughly $24,000.000 in one year, 1931, from the province of Saskatchewan alone. We are not here to indulge in quarrels between the different provinces. If some provinces are to receive substantial benefits from the fiscal policy of this country, benefits in equal measure should be conferred on other parts of the country. So far as I am concerned, I do not believe the maritimes and Alberta are getting through the fiscal policy of this dominion anything commensurate with what the central portion receives. What I rose to say was that, by means of the commission set up by this government, it is proposed I hope, so to speak, to equalize in various ways the benefits of the fiscal policy of Canada to its various provinces. We from Saskatchewan expect that our provincial government will present to that commission for consideration proposals calculated to give that province a greater measure of fairness of treatment somewhat similar to what has been granted here to the maritimes and Alberta in respect of coal. I hope that hon. members from other parts of Canada will

Supply-Lands, Parks and Forests
support us in, asking for a fair deal for Saskatchewan, since we are no less willing that Alberta and other parts of Canada shall also receive a square deal.

Oh, Saskatchewan!
Always Saskatchewan.
The hon. member for Lethbridge asked a moment ago how much money had been spent in Saskatchewan by way of subventions on coal.
Just for last year.

For the calendar year 1936 the amount was slightly over $38,000. I suggest that as it is six o'clock we should let this item stand. I wish to get the information for which my right hon. friend has asked, and we can resume discussion of this item somewhat later.
In the meantime the minister will speak a kindly word to those who should be more amenable to discipline than they are.

Will the minister get some information with regard to whether subventions clash?
Item stands.

Lands, Parks and Forests Branch
Dominion lands, seed grain, mining lands, ordnance, admiralty and public lands, salaries and expenses, et cetera, $60,060.
What is the reason for such a large decrease in this vote?
The fact that we are economizing, for one thing. In the second place, the amount of work is being steadily reduced year by year. That is the explanation given me; I asked the same question myself.
Would the minister explain what the present position is with respect to seed grain? I thought we were pretty well out of that.
There is quite a considerable amount in. outstanding accounts which are being collected.
The former government made provision for wiping off a lot of them.

Not these. These go back to 1908 and indeed further. They are old
balances of seed grain advances made by the dominion government in some instances over thirty-five years ago. These claims are being adjusted by commissions which have been set up in each of the provinces for that purpose. The federal government representatives come from the officers of the soldier settlement board. Alberta has one representative; so has Saskatchewan, and I think there is another from Manitoba. Slowly and steadily we are getting these adjustments made.
Then there is the handling of the ordnance lands. Practically all the lands owned by the federal government for federal government purposes, such as ordnance lands and lands used by other departments, revert to the Department of Mines and Resources, when not being used by the departments which originally secured them, and we administer these lands.

Can the minister tell the committee whether in British Columbia the department is cooperating with the provincial government, for example in conservation and the planting of trees? The provincial government has on foot, extensive schemes, such as reforestation.
That comes under the next item. If my hon. friend will raise the question then, we shall deal with it.
Is there any revenue derived from ordnance lands, situated along the great lakes or in other places?

Yes, there is some. I recall one ease particularly, I believe in Halifax, where some ordnance lands were leased to people who wished to use them for summer resort purposes. The basis is 6 per cent of the value of the land.
And any taxes which may be paid.
Yes, and in some cases the lands are sold, if they are no longer required, and the revenues of course revert to the crown.
How much of last year's vote was used?
I cannot answer that question now. We have information covering only nine months of the fiscal year, which does not end until March 31. The expectation is that the vote will be practically exhausted.

Has the minister the
figures to the end of 1936?
No, not here.

The minister stated that some ordnance lands are sold if they are thought to be no longer needed by the department. Can he state what the general policy of the

Supply-Lands, Parks and Forests
department is in regard to the sale of ordnance lands? I know that in certain places along the great lakes considerable tracts of ordnance lands are held which, as far as my judgment goes, are of very little value from a military standpoint. Could the minister give a general statement as to the policy of the department in keeping or disposing of these lands?

The first thing the department has to be satisfied about is that the lands will not be required at any future date for military purposes. Once that is settled, I understand the practice is to get an appraisal of the lands, and if they are under lease the lessee is given the first opportunity to buy at the appraised price. If he does not want them, we try to sell or lease to whoever might be interested. Briefly, that is the policy.

I know certain areas along
lake Erie. The shore of lake Erie is quite suitable for summer resort purposes. Along that shore there are considerable areas of land which from time to time would have been the subject of negotiation if the department had been ready to sell. I think a considerable revenue might have been derived from the sale of those lands but unfortunately, as far as I am aware, up to the present the department has not considered or approved such sales. I am not a military man and I do not know just what is necessary for defence, but these lands seem to be of very little value to the department. I would suggest to the minister that when reasonable offers are made in these cases, the department might very seriously consider selling some of this land.

The last six or seven
years have not been particularly auspicious ones for selling land or anything else. I think the practice of having a fair appraisal made of these lands and endeavouring to get that value out of the sale is sound. I do not want to put myself into such a position that my hon. friend, for instance, might come along another year and say I had squandered the public patrimony by selling these lands for less than their value.

I must differ with my
hon. friend; I think the minister should hesitate before selling these lands. My experience, in looking into these matters from time to time, was that frequently the crown required a piece of land for a particular purpose, only to find that the land was gone. Take quarantine stations, for instance; take lands that were set aside for one purpose

and used for another. To lease them is one thing; to part with them is another. My view was and is that it is highly desirable not to part with the title to lands which have been set aside for the crown, for one never knows when the crown may require a piece of vacant land. If the crown has the title to that land, with the power of resumption on due notice being given, it is able to utilize the public domain without any substantial expense. I have in mind a very definite case in which I saw the crown part with a piece of land; then, some ten or fifteen years later, another piece of land had to be acquired by expropriation. I have in mind a case in which one of our great corporations sold a three-quarter section of land at a fair price and ultimately had to buy it back at three or four times that price, because of changed conditions.
My observation, Mr. Chairman, as well as my experience, is that many of these lands set aside as ordnance lands have become particularly useful to the crown for purposes not at all connected with military operations or necessities. In these days when land is required so frequently for the purposes of the Department of Agriculture and various other departments, I suggest that it might be desirable to establish by regulation a policy that land should be leased and not sold so that the power of resumption on the giving of due notice would be always with the crown. I offer these suggestions to the minister and the committee only as a result of my observations with respect to these lands, and if that is the case during the span of one man's life how important will it become over a period of many years. The retention of land, with the title vested in the crown, in the future will be found a sound policy, and those who desire to lease the land for a period of years under conditions that will protect the interests of the crown may be permitted to do so.

I may say that I very largely agree with the observations made by my right hon. friend. As a matter of fact, I am advised that the sales are very few indeed; the practice is to lease the land, which I think is the sounder practice. If the lands can be made available in that way to those who may have some use for them for a period of years, whether for summer resort or other purposes, there is a continuing revenue to the crown.

Item agreed to.
