R esources-Forests
development of scientific management methods; forest protection studies, technical and economic investigations of forest industries; the operation of forest experiment stations, demonstration forests, and forest products laboratories; cooperative undertakings in forestry and forest products, etc., $268,300.

I wonder whether the minister would have time to answer my question now. I asked if the dominion is doing anything in British Columbia by way of scientific methods of conservation, in conjunction with the provincial government which, as the minister knows, is very much interested in this question and which is doing a great piece of work.

The federal department maintains a forest products Laboratory in Vancouver, for the purpose of examining into the values and properties of the various types of timber, and their uses in a commercial way. I understand that my hon. friend inquired also if we were assisting in reforestation or afforestation in cooperation with the provincial government. That work is being left to the provincial government, and our activities in British Columbia are confined pretty much to the work done in the laboratory.

I desire to make a few observations, and I trust that the committee and the minister will pardon me for speaking so frequently, but I happen to be the only representative on my side of the house from the province of Alberta. Perhaps otherwise I would not speak about these matters.
During my absence I took occasion to look into the work of afforestation and reforestation in New Zealand and Australia. As to reforestation, I think this work may be fairly left to nature, for nature has been better at reforesting countries than man has been. For instance, in the areas which are contiguous to the Gatineau it has been found that over a period of half a century there has been a fair growth of spruce from natural causes, through the seedlings that have been distributed by the winds in the ordinary way. In other areas near these rivers spruce has come to a fair size in sixty and seventy years. Broadly speaking, it requires nearly a century to get the results that are aimed at. Practically every year we denude five million acres of pulpwood and ship the newsprint out of this country, and this is without taking into consideration what we utilize here. Five million acres constitute quite a large area. That is largely on the Atlantic side, though some of that work is done on the Pacific side as well. As I have said, this is a very substantial area, and probably it is increasing.
If we leave reforestation to nature, then the question of afforestation becomes more
important. In New Zealand there are private enterprises which have organized companies with large capital for the purpose of carrying on afforestation operations, and they have spent millions of pounds to that end. I passed one plantation in which there were some seven or eight or ten million trees. I went into the forest for the purpose of seeing how they were growing, and I talked to a gentleman who had been in charge of those operations for many years. I brought back with me a board made from a tree that had grown from a seedling in thirty-four years. That was in New Zealand, where growth is very rapid; of course we have no such rapidity of growth in this country. I realize that the distinct difference between reforestation and afforestation is something that we in Canada must keep in mind. There are in this country vast areas of land that might be usefully planted with seedlings, but the division of responsibility between the dominion and the provinces becomes very acute when one comes to consider the matter from any angle one pleases. We have no timber lands now belonging to the dominion, except in the Northwest Territories, and other territories under federal administration. The lands that are being denuded of trees for the export of newsprint are lands belonging to the provinces, and not to the dominion. The question of reforestation is a matter which one would think would engage the serious attention of provincial authorities.
With respect to afforestation, in western Canada we have carried on an educational campaign during at least the last half century. When I first went to western Canada, now nearly forty years ago, seedlings were being distributed every year from the farm at Indian Head, and elsewhere, and the many farms which we now see on the prairies with clumps of poplars about them, forming wind breaks and shelters, were thus protected by the seedlings distributed from the farm at Indian Head. In addition to that farm, there are others from which these seedlings have been distributed.
It seems to me, under present conditions, that is the only work the dominion can properly carry on, for we have no areas to set aside for afforestation. We have no areas over which we may have control, except the ordnance land about which we were speaking a few minutes ago, lands in the Northwest Territories, the lands which are vested in us as part of our experimental farms, and other areas which have fallen into our hands. I certainly believe we should cooperate with the provinces to the extent of our ability, but to suggest that we can undertake a policy
Supply-R esources-Forests

of afforestation in the various provinces of the dominion is to suggest that we could interfere with them in the administration of their property, and undertake to direct policies of which they are so jealous, and have been all through the years.
Therefore when we came to the question of afforestation indicated in the item, I was curious to have the minister indicate what he had in mind, and what the break-up of the item might be. If, as is the case in Australia, we had only one central government, the problem could easily be dealt with, but accepting the situation as it now stands it seems to me perfectly clear that all we can do is to give such assistance as is within our powers, by reason of our ownership and operation of experimental farms, and the operation of our laboratories. We have one in Vancouver and one in the east seeking to determine how best we may be able to secure the continuance of what is indeed one of our most wasting assets, namely our timber.
No thoughtful man who has read the history of the United States of America for the last hundred years can fail to be profoundly affected by the situation which has developed in Canada. It is all right to look at those magnificent trees in British Columbia, but when one realizes that some of them were a fairly good size before Columbus discovered America he begins to realize that a policy of afforestation or reforestation will bring no results during lifetimes of many, many generations, so far as Douglas fir is concerned. With, regard to spruce, the condition is somewhat different, and with regard to hardwood it is still more different. I suggest that the problem confronting the Canadian people in connection with their timber assets is one of profound importance. The wasting of this great asset, which cannot readily be made available again, is something which should engage the attention of those who reap revenue from it, namely the provincial authorities. We cannot impose our will upon them; much less should we endeavour to do so, but to the extent of our ability I think we should indicate to them, as has been done in the past, through the department which has knowledge of the experiments and knowledge which has come from information gained by representatives at various conventions throughout the world, how we can within a reasonable time secure a regrowth of timber which would be available for use. That has been done in Sweden and in other countries.
For instance, a certain type of poplar may be used for matches. With veneer knives they

take many, many thousands of match ends off one particular tree. In Sweden they have done a great deal of work in connection with the reforestation of that particular type of tree, and in this country it seems to me we could do a great deal in the valley of the Ottawa, for instance, where that particular type of tree grows well. But just how one can adjust the federal government into the picture, so as to ensure something like a reasonable return for the effort, is a matter of great difficulty. Certainly I have seen but little evidence on the part of any of the provinces of a desire for the dominion even to suggest to them what they might do. That is the reason I should like the minister to indicate what he means by the item.

As my right hon. friend has said, it is quite true that the control of the forest areas is now within the provinces. I believe at the present time there is a growing appreciation of the importance of sound methods of conservation and harvesting. The work the federal government carries on under the vote is confined largely to the stations it has established!. Perhaps the committee would be interested to know where they are located. There is one in New Brunswick, known as the Acadian forest experimental area, covering an area of thirty-eight square miles. Then at Valcartier in Quebec there is a small one of seven and a half square miles. In the Peta-wawa area of northern Ontario there is an area of one hundred square miles; in Manitoba there is the Duck mountain forest experimental station with an area of approximately thirty-six square miles, and in Alberta, west of Calgary, there is the Kananaskis station with an area of sixty-three square miles. As I said a few moments ago, experimental work is done at these stations. For instance, study is carried on as to how best the growth of trees may be promoted. Early last summer I had an opportunity of visiting the Petawawa station and observing the work done there. It is carried out along definite scientific lines. In fact, the work carried on by the various experimental stations is of the same kind as that done by the experimental farms of the various provinces.
The data gathered from the experimental work is made available to the provinces and to private owners of timber who are operating pulp-mills, sawmills or other timber processing plants. I agree with the right hon. gentleman that there is a need of impressing upon the people generally the wisdom of sound conservation policies with respect to our forest wealth. It is only within very recent years

Supply-Resources-Forests
that the importance of this asset has been realized. Several weeks ago I had an opportunity of attending the annual meeting of the Canadian Pulp and Paper Association, and in my discussions with the managers of companies connected with the operations I found them very much alive to the need of sound methods not only of harvesting the crop but of maintaining the supply.
What Sweden has done is, as was indicated by the right hon. gentleman, an illustration of what can be achieved by sound methods. Undoubtedly we have been slow in realizing the importance of our forests, but I do believe that in an increasing measure it is being realized to-day. I attribute much of the increased interest in sound conservation policies to the work being done by the dominion in the areas to which I referred.

And by the Canadian
Forestry Association.

And by the Canadian
Forestry Association. The work done by the Indian Head experimental farm in western Canada has been most valuable; it has been mostly along the lines of providing shelter belts and sheltered areas for homesteaders and farmers on what are sometimes described as the baldheaded prairies. This is very important work. Were the country in a more favourable position, I should like to see more money provided for this work. I should like to mention one interesting experiment which I saw being carried on in the laboratory at Montreal.
Mr. MacNICOiL: Where is that laboratory?

In the university grounds
at Montreal. I may say that this building was erected by the pulp and paper people. Experimental work is carried on in the grinding of woods and the various processes in the manufacturing of paper.

Is that not under the
direction of McGill University?

Partly. The experiment in which I was so much interested had to do with the production of a beautiful grade of paper from a mixture of hardwood pulp and softwood pulp. I think such experiments are very valuable. In a general way, that is the work being carried on under this vote, and I have no hesitation whatever in saying that this is one of the most important phases of the work carried on by this branch of the department.

Mr. Chairman, the minister has partly answered a question I intended to ask in connection with the laboratory, that is where it is located and what work it is doing. I am glad to hear that there is such an institution although I had not known there was. I made a special trip to Madison, Wisconsin, where perhaps the largest forest products laboratory in the world is located. This is a magnificent glass and concrete building costing in the neighbourhood of $14,000,000. The building was erected by the United States government for carrying on general forestry work. Everyone realizes that the manufacture of forest products creates employment for thousands of men, and I endorse whatever the minister has in mind with reference to the preservation of forests, laboratory work and other matters of that kind.
I noticed that at Madison they had seven different departments. The first department has to do with finding additional uses for wood and the elimination of waste in connection with the manufacture of wood products. As someone said a moment ago, there is an enormous waste in this dominion. It would seem as though our supplies of wood were thought to be inexhaustible, but they certainly are not, as one can see when he goes around the country. The second department deals with the strength of woods and the study of what wood could be best suited for particular purposes. I found this work very interesting. For instance, they studied the different types of wood to be used in the making of crates. In many instances a heavy wood is used where a lighter wood would provide better service. Reports are sent out all over the country to manufacturers and the results have been tremendous. I was told that they save the manufacturing industry in the United States an average of $4,000,000 per year.
The third department has to do with the processing of woods, a matter of great interest to the furniture manufacturers. Many improvements have been suggested to these people in regard to the type of dry kiln to use, and they claim a saving of about $10,000,000 per year. A study of construction problems is being made. To my mind this is very important. As anyone connected with the industry knows, steel is making rapid inroads into the realm of lumber. By increasing the use of wood they hope to provide more employment in Sawmills and planing mills throughout the country. Another department has to do with the best methods of treating woods to make them more fire resisting. Another department has to do with the ingredients to be used in paints to increase the life of wood.
Supply-R esources-Fores ts

Does this laboratory in Montreal carry on similar investigations to the best of its ability? I realize that it could not compete with a $14,000,000 plant, but if it is doing any work along this line, it deserves the serious support of this committee.

I think most of the experiments referred to by my hon. friend are carried on at the Ottawa and Vancouver laboratories. The problems considered in Montreal are those more closely associated with the pulp and paper industry. They make analyses of pulps and consider the absorption of alcohol on pulps. They classify all pulps by selective screening and they conduct studies as to the best methods of grinding woods. They consider all things which enter into and vitally touch the pulp and paper industry. I am informed that, as a result of the work carried on in this laboratory, suggestions have been made which have materially reduced the cost of producing paper. This is a very important matter at the present time. As hon. members are aware, our large market for pulp and paper is in the United States, which coun*-try has vast areas of southern pine. We know that experimental work is being carried on in that country with the object of converting those pine woods into pulp and paper. It is, I think, vastly important that we in Canada should keep ourselves up to date in all the information which touches upon this subject; at the same time we should carry on our own experimental work for the benefit of our pulp and paper manufacturers, and that is the work which has been carried on mainly in the laboratory in Montreal.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, just a word on the point mentioned by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) and also by the minister (Mr. Crerar). I think this discussion is of vital importance to any man who loves a tree and who appreciates the relationship between tree life and human life. Although in this chamber we have not control over the forest resources of Canada except to the limited degree indicated by the leader of the opposition and the minister, we do represent the people of Canada; and if the history of the world teaches us anything it teaches us this, that if tree life goes, human life cannot long be sustained in the area thus denuded. That is borne out on the pages of history. While we cannot control these matters, we can by the words uttered here stimulate in the minds of Canadians a greater regard for the renewing of these resources which are being destroyed year by year and destroyed more, I believe, by fire and insect pests than by the extent to which we are using 
them commercially. To a very great degree I believe that is true. Nature will do a lot herself if she is given a chance.
I remember during my early life in the west that the tree line was a great deal further north than it is now, particularly in eastern Saskatchewan. The leader of the opposition I am sure will remember that the Canadian Pacific railway main line passing through by Broadview traversed practically bare country thirty years ago, but the trees have gradually crept southward. Why? Because the prairie fires which destroyed them formerly have been stopped by the cultivation of farms. Let us do all we can to stimulate in the minds of our people the need to cooperate with nature in replenishing these great stores which mean so much, not merely in the way of an asset in manufacturing something, but also in relation to the preservation of the means whereby human beings can live in this country. The great problems of erosion referred to by the leader of the opposition, which are so apparent in the United States but are not, as yet, so apparent here, are apparent, nevertheless, in some parts and will become increasingly so if forest growth disappears, and to the extent that we can stimulate public opinion to appreciate the importance of the problem-and it is very largely a matter of individual trees-to that extent we are doing a useful work for our country. I have no doubt that the expression of opinions given here to-night will find an echo across the dominion, and once public opinion is aroused then proper measures must be taken by the proper authorities to deal with the matter.
From	the	standpoint	of	this governmentand	of	this	parliament	we	can continue to
carry on the nursery work, the work in the parks, and the laboratory work to which the minister has referred, but so far as control is concerned that very definitely is in the hands of the provincial authorities, except in areas which are definitely owned outright by the dominion.

Mr. Chairman, I should like	to	add	my voice	to	what has beensaid	by	the	leader of	the	opposition (Mr. Bennett), the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning). I think this is one of the most important items in the estimates to come before the house this session. In the past we have not paid as much attention to protecting our forests as we ought to have done. The province of British Columbia had at one time the finest forest, I suppose, to be found anywhere in the world. We thought we had a forest which was inexhaustible, and we thought
Supply-R esources-Forests
that only a very few years ago. But from studies and investigations made within the last few years it is estimated, by what is considered to be competent authority, that within twenty-five years the accessible commercial forest in British Columbia will have disappeared. Not only will its commercial value have disappeared, but many evils will have taken the place of the asset we now have. It is largely a matter of protection. I have watched forests grow, and all they want is a chance to grow. I was greatly surprised a few years ago, when I went back to that part of the maritihie provinces where I was brought up, to find that what was in those early days cultivated fields is now a forest of trees with some twenty-five to thirty feet of growth.
The leader of the opposition has referred to Sweden. I had an opportunity to visit Sweden and Norway this summer, and one of the things that surprised me, after seeing the desolation caused by forest fires in British Columbia, was to find no such areas at all in Sweden or Norway. If they have any such areas, I did not see them. I was told by people there that despite the extensive use they have made of their forests, cutting the timber for use at home and for export for over a hundred years, the forests of Sweden are greater to-day than they were a hundred years ago. To my mind that should be a lesson to us. Some way will have to be found for cooperation between the federal and provincial governments to preserve what forests we have and to give nature a chance to reproduce so that we may continue to have forests in the future.
I notice that the minister has begun to inform public opinion by radio addresses, and I hope these will continue. Let me repeat, some way will have to be found to get cooperation between the dominion and the provinces in this most essential work that is facing the people of Canada to-day.

May I ask the minister what part of this appropriation is for Peta-wawa park, and what is the number of employees there? Does the reservation extend across the Ottawa river into the province of Quebec? Is fire prevention a part of the work of the employees?

The reservation does not extend into the province of Quebec. Fire prevention is one of the subjects under constant study in the forest reserve at Petawawa. It was interesting to me on the first visit I made to one of these stations last summer to observe the methods that are followed in determining the fire hazard; for. example,
the amount of moisture in the ground under the trees is measured, and as the amount of moisture decreases the fire hazard increases. There are five permanent employees in that station. I believe that during the summer months there is additional temporary help.

How much is
the appropriation?
I do not know that I can give precisely the amount which we have appropriated. A little over $21,000 is down for Petawawa this year.

The hon. member for
Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) has said that it is for the most part a matter of protection of forests. I agree with him to a large extent, but on the other hand it must be also a matter of education. For instance, in the province of Quebec we have very rich forest reserves, and the government had for a time the idea of establishing settlers on lots which previously were very rich in trees, but the lumbermen used to cut all the wood before the settlers could reach those lots, and there was no proper division between farm lands and forest reserves. It was a great mistake, the result being that very often settlers were established on lots on which there was no timber; they could not find enough wood on their own lots to build their houses and do a little profitable trade in the wintertime. The most essential thing for sound settlement on new lots is that they should be covered with timber; then the timber can be cut by the settler and provide him with some income during the winter. At present the wood is cut mostly by lumber companies; nothing is left for the settlers and they have to rely upon direct relief for what is, at times, a very poor living. If there could be an arrangement of some kind between the dominion government and the provinces by virtue of which the settlers would be established on well-timbered lots, neither the federal government nor the provincial governments would have to pay anything for relief of settlers. At the present time the condition of the settlers is awful; most of them have been taken from the cities and placed on rocky soil in the forests, far away from civilization, and as a consequence both governments have to provide direct relief. It is an absurd situation, and I hope that some of the money included in this item will be applied to education, including education of the provincial governments, so that they may realize the value of the timber to settlers, and that our forest reserves shall not be destroyed by eager lumber merchants.
Supply-Resources-Forests

I think it is recognized
that fire is one of the most destructive elements in our forests, particularly in British Columbia. Will the minister inform us whether his department cooperates in any way with the provincial governments in fire protection? Does it make a grant or use any of this money for protective purposes? I suppose that when the lands were handed over to the provinces, the care of the timber became their sole obligation, but I should like to know whether there remains anything in the way of cooperation with the provinces for the prevention of fires.

No. Fire protection in
British Columbia and other provinces is a matter for the provinces themselves. We place at their disposal all such data and information as we gather, for instance, in our forest experimental work at the stations to which I referred a few minutes ago.
And we make a small grant to the forestry association.

As the leader of the opposition has stated, we make a grant to the forestry association,. The federal responsibility as discharged under this vote is confined to experimental work in these stations and in the laboratories and to the dissemination of information to the public in every reasonable way that we can reach them, concerning the importance of conservation, the need of guarding against fire, and similar matters. It is now fairly well ascertained that a great many forest fires originate through carelessness. Excepting those which are started, by lightning, all other causes of fire cam be prevented. It may mean a long journey to accomplish this, but we have steadily to work on public opinion to give our people a realization of the importance of exercising ordinary care to guard against fires in our forests.

Is the department carrying on any experimental work in connection with selective logging? I understand that selective logging is the system followed in, Europe, and that thereby they have succeeded to a very large extent in preserving their, forests. I do not know of any such work being carried on in British Columbia. In Oregon, in the county of Malheur, east of the coast range, they are carrying on selective logging on very considerable tracts of land and handling the work successfully. By that system they take out what is ripe and ready to cut and preserve sufficient young trees to grow a new crop in a short time. With the high lead system of logging practised in the large
[M:\ Pouliot.]
timber areas of British Columbia, they break down the trees that are of no use to them, with the result that under the present system very few trees escape. Selective logging consists in taking trees that are old enough and fit to cut, and leaving the others in the forest to grow. Are any experiments along that line being carried out?

I am advised that the department is carrying on, certain investigational work in connection with the matter raised by the hon. member for Victoria, B.C. (Mr. Tolmie). The information, which by practical illustration indicates the importance of such methods, is made available in as widespread a fashion as possible. I am certain that among many of the large companies operating in eastern Canada there is a fairly clear realization of the importance of the very point raised by the hon. member. After all, it is simply a sensible way of harvesting a crop so as not to destroy what will be the crop of the future. I can only reiterate that, after all, it is through the impact made on public opinion by the dissemination of knowledge and the application of that knowledge in a practical way on the widest possible scale, as is now being done, that the desired results will be produced.

Does the minister not think the time is fast approaching when we should take up this matter in, a large way and carry on a campaign of instruction in the areas where forests still remain, with a view of conserving our timber much better than it is being conserved at the present time?

The suggestion of my hon. friend is probably a very good one, but when I come to ask for an increased vote to spread this work even, further we have to take into account various factors. There are many demands on the public treasury. All I can say is that I think we are getting very good value for the money expended under this vote. Personally I should like to see it larger, I hope that in a few years we may be in a position to increase it, and extend the useful work which can be done in that way. Meantime we shall do the best we can with the money at our disposal.

I want to add my voice to those of others who have urged the minister to do all he possibly can to encourage people to respect their forests, and if he can shout loud enough to be heard in British Columbia it will do a great deal of good to Canada. People say that public opinion will preserve our forests. I am afraid that when the lumberman comes to a tree one thousand years old, he thinks very little

Supply-R esources-Fore s ts
about public opinion and a lot about his personal profit. They cut down these trees with high rigging and destroy whole forests as they move along, and nothing but a determined effort on the part of the dominion and the province together will set matters right in British Columbia, for that province is fast being denuded of its forests. Students of tree life tell us that the famous fir trees one thousand and more years old will not grow again in British Columbia. The abies amabilis nobilis, as I think it is called, is a tree that belongs to the past, and once cut down has no life to carry on. It is replaced by other and lighter growths, so that if we are to have some of these fine old trees preserved for those who come after us, we must educate now and educate definitely to protect our forest life. I sincerely hope the minister will do all he possibly can to see that British Columbia, of all provinces, knows more about this work.

I wish to say just a few words more, without intruding my views too much on the attention of the committee. I visited the forest of western Australia because I had heard that they were taking extreme care of that great and valuable resource. I found that foresters selected with great care the trees to be cut down and marked them, and then provision was made for planting new trees. That is the jarrah tree and the karri tree. It is true that the governments own the forests, and carry on the operation of or own the mills. In Queensland they own their forests as well, and instead of permitting them to be leased for long terms they provide that a sawmill is licensed to cut so many feet per annum, and that a competing sawmill is not placed there because no more may be cut than the quantity which they allot for that particular place. I suspect that it would be very difficult to get provincial administration in this country to look at matters in that way. One of the difficulties Canada suffers from to-day is that we have built too many pulp-mills for the purpose of meeting the market requirements of the great republic to the south; the result is that the governments of Ontario and Quebec have competed with one another in requiring the construction of pulp and paper mills as a condition attached to the leases of land, and the competition has become so fierce because of overproduction, owing to the number of mills and the limited consumption, that Canadians have been exchanging an old dollar for a new one without any corresponding return for the tremendous losses sustained by the denuding of the forest lands. I said a moment ago that five million acres of land were denuded of
trees to provide for the export of newsprint from this country last year.
I think the minister has perhaps gone a little too far in connection with the laboratory. The laboratory at Montreal is operated in a building which was constructed by the pulp and paper association on the university lands, and the late Mrs. Eddy left $200,000 for the establishment of the E. B. Eddy chair in connection with that organization. Professor Hibbert, who came from Yale and organized that staff, is responsible for the experiments carried on. There is no difficulty about the utilization of our wood; that difficulty, I think, we have mastered; our trouble is the preservation of our wood. It is true we are able to improve the quality of our pulp and the production of our papers, but is it not an odd commentary-to anticipate something which may be discussed later- that we are actually paying a drawback on paper imported-
Of the duty.

Just so-on paper imported here for the purpose of printing Canadian magazines? The budget provides for a 75 per cent drawback of the duty to be paid on paper, probably made from Canadian products, imported from the United States for the publishing of papers in Canada. That is an illustration, the most outstanding evidence of our failure to measure up to the necessities of the situation as our competing friends to the south have done. I confess I have never been quite able to understand this.
That laboratory deals with utilization, not preservation. Conservation is admirable, but let me go a step further. At Canberra one of the first things they did when they established their capital was to set up a school of forestry. With Mr. Lane Poole I spent as interesting an hour as any I spent while away, looking over an exhibit of the woods of the world, and I found there as fine an exhibit of Canadian woods as could be found anywhere in Canada. But what struck me is the point referred to a moment ago by one hon. member, namely the question of destruction of wood by insects. I was amazed to find the extent to which that problem is being dealt with; the illustrations of it from every part of the world were striking. For instance, in one part of Australia wooden sleepers or railroad ties are impossible because they would be eaten at once by the white ants. In northern Rhodesia they use teak. As soon as the tie is cut is it immersed in a strong bath of insecticide; after it has been boiled in this arsenic solution it is put



Supply[DOT]-Resources-Forests
into boiling tar, and in this way it is made impervious to either the action of the weather or insects. In other places they use steel ties entirely. But when one thinks of that magnificent teakiwood being used for that purpose, one has some difficulty in believing that conservation is being carried to the extent it might be.
As to fire, I was astonished at the amount spent in protecting forests from being burnt, and the extent of the precautions taken. They have forest rangers everywhere, telephone communication linking them together; many of our people in Canada are doing much the same sort of work. The minister referred to fires started by lightning, but I am told that, taking the world over, the fires that owe their origin to lightning are probably very few.
Not very many, but some.

Careless men, and somestart fires. Measures are certainly taken to guard against sparks from railway engines and guard against sparks from railway engines and that sort of thing. Now could we not do something to take a more advanced position with respect to conservation as distinguished from utilization? -In connection with insects and parasites and matters of that sort I think we could give assistance under the constitution, under our broad and general powers in connection with agriculture. But marking trees and carrying on propaganda in that regard would be extremely difficult to accomplish in this country, having regard to the fact, as mentioned by the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Taylor), that unfortunately people having leases of our forest areas in British Columbia do not in many instances reside in this country; they are absentee lessees, who are now operating leased lands in Canada and shipping the resultant lumber not only to the United States but to various parts of the world. That is a factor which it is beyond our power to consider, except perhaps through an export duty, which we still would have power to impose if we so desired. I remember one gentleman who urged upon me at one time the desirability of considering whether or not the time had come for the regulation of exports from British Columbia in such a way as would prevent the exhaustion of those resources, which exhaustion he believed would . occur within the lifetime of his grandchild. That may be an exaggerated view with respect to the matter.
That being so, Mr. Chairman, I agree with the minister that our only hope of accomplishing anything as a dominion must be through the creation of a sound public opinion. If a campaign such as was suggested by the hon.

member for Victoria, B.C., were to be carried on, we would have to be sure beforehand that it would not be met with that negative attitude on the part of the province concerned which would make it absolutely useless to make the attempt. That is our real difficulty. For instance, there is the question of the cutting and exporting of pulpwood. Most of our crown leases in the provinces contain a provision that pulpwood cannot be exported, but one has only to read the newspapers to see that in some instances that provision has been relaxed, for many reasons. We had an inquiry into the matter, as I dare say the minister will remember; I have no doubt he was in the house at the time that commission reported. While there is a statute that permits a prohibition to be enforced by order in council, no action has ever been taken to prevent the export of pulpwood, because in practice this has been found to constitute a very desirable market for those who, if it were not for that power of export, would be paid less money than they think they should receive.
Somewhat less, at any rate.

The report of the commission was along that line, and the old government-I am not sure whether or not it was in the days of the union government- took power to pass an order in council prohibiting that export. Then there is, for instance, the movement of logs out of this country. I think it will be remembered that during the days of Sir Oliver Mowat certain action was taken in the province of Ontario to lessen that evil as they saw it. I believe some action was taken that lessened the possibility of the movement of these magnificent logs across the sound from British Columbia to the United States and to some, though not to a very great extent, we have endeavoured to limit the movement of logs not only to Japan but also to Australia, in order that in our own country we might have the work of producing the lumber from these logs.
All these are problems that indicate how we might cooperate, the dominion with the provinces, to bring about a result that I think is of the utmost importance. A moment ago the Minister of Finance had something to say about the tree, and I am sure hon. members of this committee have read a great deal about it. Mr. Barker-I think that is the name; it is either Barker or Baker-has written so beautifully about the tree man and the trees of Great Britain as almost to make one feel that they are living things. I know when I see a great tree fall to the ground

Supply-Resources-Forests
it always gives me a pang. A tree always seems to be something for which one has a sort of human feeling. Some of the old trees, such as those in the parks around Windsor and the tree beneath which old Lobengula used to sit when he administered justice, recall times so long past and events so important that one almost looks upon them as living things which have taken a vital part in the history of the country itself. Trees have played such a vital part that perhaps as a committee we can do nothing better by this brief discussion than help men and women in all parts of Canada to realize the debt we owe to nature and nature's God for giving us this rich heritage of trees as a trust, not to exhaust within our lifetime but so to utilize that the generations which come after us may have reason to look back with pride upon the fact that we had some sense of obligation and preserved something to them even as the past handed it to us.

If next year the minister will ask for a greater allotment of money for this purpose I shall gladly support him, because I feel keenly the need for conserving our forest growth. I know in my own province there are areas that once were covered with trees that are now completely denuded, and frequently those hills are of no value at all at the present time. It seems to me that in many cases we might, in some way or another, gain control of these hilly areas and have them replanted. If we did that, we would be better off both as a dominion and as a province.
There are several matters that have occurred to my mind, which perhaps it would be as well for me to tell the minister about now. because otherwise I might forget. Probably he has thought of all these matters also, but in travelling around the country this summer there were a few things that struck me forcibly. In the first place, in Alberta we suffered great loss because of forest fires which resulted from the extremely dry season. That came to my mind particularly when I saw beautiful areas around the Waterton lakes park and in other districts completely spoiled by fire. Those areas will not be the same again for perhaps one hundred and fifty years. It occurred to me that it might be wise in future for the dominion to take on what I might call an emergency force of wardens who could be transferred from one part of the country to another, so that they might be stationed in that part of the country where there happened to be a drought. I know in Alberta we could have saved great wooded areas of untold value if the fire fighting forces had been 31111-87A
perhaps quadrupled just during the two or three weeks or so of extreme dryness. I noticed also, when I went across the line by way of Logan pass, that on the other side of the line they lost very heavily also, so evidently there was no comparative lack of care on our part. It was most pathetic to see these areas; it gave me a pang, as the right hon. leader of the opposition said, to see what had happened to those areas which had been so beautiful just the year before.
Then another matter came to my attention. I heard from one who was intimately connected with the logging business in British Columbia that there are logging concerns which are very destructive in the way they take out trees. One man to whom I was speaking on the subject was a student of forestry at one of the institutions in British Columbia. He told me of one concern that he saw which was destroying six trees for every tree it took out, and this was going on just as quickly as high-powered machinery and organized crews could go through the forest. This gentleman told me that the trees thus destroyed were really more of a loss than the trees cut down, because new trees would grow in place of those cut down but those that were destroyed would stand for many years, unsightly, in the way, simply wasted. I thought notice should be taken of this destruction; it seemed to me that stern measures should be applied, by strategy if need be, to put a stop to that sort of thing, and the words of the hon. member for Nanaimo brought the matter to my mind with even greater force. Something should be done now, before parliament meets again.
I believe the suggestion advanced by the right hon. leader of the opposition would be a good thing. If necessary we might adopt measures that will stop the export of these trees. If we cannot redeem the leases or force these men to sell them back to us in order to preserve these priceless treasures that have been left to us as a heritage which I think we should pass on, we might very well consider taking that step. When I was a university student in Edmonton there were many wooded areas close to that city. I had come from the plains, and I used to tell the farmers there that they would regret some day the wasteful cutting down of trees. I urged that at least they leave a belt eight feet wide along the fence lines, so that they would have wind breaks in time of need. They paid no attention in 1909 or 1910, but surely to-day those farmers are suffering from the very condition I told them about. They denuded the country. During the four years I attended the university there was only one

Supply-Resources-Forests
wind high enough to blow off a person's hat, but to-day if one goes to Edmonton he will find drifting snow and soil blown about almost as would happen in the south. They were unwise to cut down so many of the trees.
It used to occur to me that the government would have been well advised in those days to have preserved one-quarter out of every section, and to have refrained from throwing it open for settlement. That ground could have been kept as a kind of permanent reserve, would have served as a home for birds, helped to conserve the soil and to conserve animal life, and would have prevented the denudation of the country to a point where high winds are possible. If the minister has not already taken such precaution, I would suggest it would be well to cooperate with the other departments and see whether or not something like that could be done, so that the great areas which are being opened in some sections may have that protection.
Another point which has occurred to me is this: Areas which once were park lands are being returned to the government because, as we say, the people cannot make good. Perhaps frost or some other factor is prevents ing them. As the land goes back to the government for taxes, it seems to me that a sort of planned economy would lead the federal government in conjunction with the provincial governments to take steps to take over a quarter of every section, have it replanted and held for the future. Even where the land is not coming back to the government, it might be wise to buy a quarter. There are quarters which are not much good for farming. North of Edmonton I found areas where trees had been cut down, which areas have been shown to be entirely worthless for farming purposes. After cutting the trees down they found there was sand, much the same as is found in some parts of Quebec, with a thin layer of good soil over the top of it. The good soil was quickly exhausted, and all that remains is worthless. The lands could have been redeemed or reconditioned by the provincial or federal governments.
Last year I was invited to go to Shawinigan Falls, where I saw something which greatly impressed me. I am told that the Shawinigan power people are presenting the town each year with a piece of land which has been denuded of trees, but which has been replanted with young trees. It was one of the most pleasant sights I had ever seen to drive out from Shawinigan Falls to see slopes, which had been denuded and would have been unsightly, beautifully planted with trees growing for the delight and profit of the future. Probably we could encourage other companies to do likewise.

One further point I believe has not been mentioned to the minister. I am wondering whether it would be a good thing for him to go into Banff national park and examine closely the situation with respect to beavers. I believe it is known to hon. members that in some parts of the west beavers have increased to such an extent that they are attacking fine trees and destroying them. We value the beaver, but I fancy a good colony of beaver would be worth less than the plot of trees they would destroy. The matter was brought to my attention quite forcibly by men whose names I should not mention. I thought it would be well to draw the situation to the attention of the minister.
Once again may I express my great satisfaction that the minister is making an effort to conserve our forests. May I state that I am in agreement with hon. members who have expressed enthusiasm for the conservation of our forests, and I would urge that the movement be pressed forward with the greatest of energy so that in future we may preserve and possibly increase our forest wealth.

Mr. Chairman, for the last half hour the discussion this evening has been interesting, but I should like to advise the minister not to take too seriously much of what has been said. After all, trees are like any other crop. If they are not harvested when they are mature they go to waste, as will any other growth. Not only do they go to waste themselves, but after becoming rotten at the core some of them are blown down by the winds and, in falling, they take other trees with them. The result is that often fire may break out and destroy a whole forest. If trees are not used, except for scenic and beauty purposes, not only will they deteriorate but they will clutter up the land and prevent other trees from growing.
I believe we should encourage the growth of further supplies of trees when those which are now mature are harvested but there is a good deal of sentimentality when we talk about trees, and sometimes the question is not thoroughly understood. A little while ago an hon. member complained that pulpwood had been shipped out of the country. When pulpwood was being shipped out of Canada the men handling it were making a comfortable living. During the past five or six years, when there was no pulpwood going out of Canada and no sale for it, the men who were formerly handling it were taking out firewood and in some cases selling it as low as eighty cents a cord, in order to make a bare living. They were selling firewood at that price where formerly they had been able to get $5 or $8

Supply-Resources-Forests
a cord for pulpwood, depending upon where it was shipped. A Canadian mill would pay $5, whereas an American mill buying pulpwood from patented lands would pay $8 for the same quality.
I do not think this country has any moral right, as indeed it has no legal right, to the ownership of pulpwood. I suppose it has the legal right to restrict export, but I think it has no more moral right to restrict the export of pulpwood by those who own it than to prohibit the export of cattle or hogs or grain or any manufactured goods produced in Canada.
There is something which can be done under the vote, and I am satisfied the minister and his department are doing good work along this line. I believe it was the leader of the opposition who spoke about the laboratory at Montreal, and what it has done. But it seemed to me he appeared to be of opinion that the laboratory had pretty well served its purpose, and that we knew pretty well now how to utilize our forest wealth. There is one part of our forest wealth we do not understand adequately, and that is the question of jack pine in pulpwood, to be mixed with spruce. I know there is a constantly increasing percentage of jack pine, and I would not go so far as to say there are not other woods being added to spruce. If we can devise a formula, or if a scientist at the laboratory in Montreal or elsewhere can devise one whereby a constantly increasing percentage of jack pine, poplar and other woods could be used with spruce, it would be worth all the laboratory costs for maintenance. I appreciate the fact that the department and the minister are interested in this particular matter.
After all that has been said about the , exhaustion of the spruce tree, we are finding that it is not correot. Ten years ago there was quite a campaign to secure the prohibition of export of pulpwood from Canada. We have more spruce to-day suitable for pulp-making than we had a't that time, because we have not been using spruce much for a number of years. We are oversupplied. At the present time our exports of forest products have greatly increased and, if my memory serves me correctly, are above the previous high record. It is true prices are not as high as we would like to have them; nevertheless the forest is providing a living for a great many workers, and it is helping as much as any other branch of industry to bring Canada back to prosperity. Another reason why there is more spruce or pulpwood is that it has been growing very fast.
An hon. member on this side of the chamber said a little while ago that he did not like to listen to western members talking on behalf of the maritime provinces. I do not want to do that, but I think it is within the memory of many of us here that a noted timber conservationist from the maritime provinces was in the habit of advertising the fact that down there a spruce tree would grow about an inch or an inch and a half in width per year provided conditions were favourable. I know that trees do grow extremely fast down there, but it must not be forgotten that even in the interior, where the winters are longer and the summers shorter and rainfall less-these are the factors that govern the growth of trees-the growth is quite rapid provided fire is kept out of the forests. If we can do that, they will grow fast enough.
I think it was the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) who advocated the reforestation of lands which had come back into public ownership. That would be fine provided these lands had been covered with timber at one time, but if an attempt is made at the reforestation of prairie lands which were never meant to support timber, then the effort will be only a waste of time and money. An hon. member stated a little while ago that he was amazed at the destruction of trees in the district around Edmonton and he wondered why the farmers could not have left a strip of trees around their land. Apparently he was under a misapprehension or was not thoroughly familiar with the situation. These trees were probably matured and if they were not cut down or utilized in some other way, they would only blow down. Just as soon as you start in clearing the land, that is what is going to happen. Trees that grow in the middle of a forest have not the long tap roots to anchor them as have trees growing more thinly, and unless they are cut down, and marketed if a market is available, they are simply wasted.
There is another phase to this question. There are dirt highways in the rural parts of western Canada, and even in eastern Canada, alongside of which are many trees. These trees prevent the roads from drying up after a rain and in many cases automobiles and other vehicles are stuck in the mud. These trees serve no useful purpose. Someone else advocated a system of marking trees. I have never been a lumberman, but from my many years of observation I am sure that you will get nothing but grief if you suggest to the lumbermen that a young fellow just out of school should go in and mark the trees

Supply-Resources-Forests
*which they should cut. He is going to tell such a man to learn his business. It is true that we must have regulations, and we must *enforce them, but that is not the way to do it. The question of inseot pests is very important. I hope the minister will be able to secure sufficient parasites to combat this menace which is endangering the spruce and other trees of this country.

Mr. Chairman, I was very much interested in the remarks of the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. McLean) and his statement that trees should be considered as a crop. My experience in New Brunswick has been that three or four crops will be harvested in a year if the lumbermen are not watched. I think the efforts made by this government and the provincial government to preserve our forests have been fairly successful. Our history in New Brunswick shows that at one time our great forests were completely depleted. If it were not for the efforts of the governments of the last few years, we would not have the great source of revenue we now have in our forests. It is not my intention to make a speech on forest conservation, but I should like to ask the minister how much of this vote is being set aside for the development of the area of twenty-eight square miles in New Brunswick to which he referred? I know this area was being developed a few years ago as a relief project but it was stopped last year. I was wondering whether the work is still being carried on by the department and I should like to know what stage the development has reached.
The experimental station buildings are completed. The total amount appropriated out of this vote for this station is $14,463.
Are the buildings completed which were to be erected in this area?
I am informed that the building necessary to carry on the work have been practically completed.
Could the minister give us the damage by forest fires in 1936 as compared with 1935??
I am sorry, but I am unable to give my hon. friend that information. It is a pretty large order. We shall probably have it in time, but we do not have it at the moment.
It would be only an estimate.
Are the forests of Canada being depleted or is the natural growth equal to the cut made each year?
That is an almost impossible question to answer, except by way of a very general estimate. I would hesitate even to pass any opinion upon it.
Does the minister not think we should know?

Probably we should know, but that would involve an extensive survey of the forest wealth of Canada. We do know that there are very large areas in which the trees are growing larger all the time and coming to a point where they will be of commercial value. In lumbering and woods operations the wood most readily accessible is the wood that is taken first. I have flown over much of British Columbia and I know there are great forests inland from the coast. It is doubtful whether on the present basis of prices this wood could be made available due to the cost of moving it out. We know that in the northern parts of Manitoba and Saskatchewan and in many parts of Alberta and Ontario there are areas where forests are being produced. This process is going on all the time. I am sure that my right hon. friend, the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett), will recall that thirty years ago in the area between Portage la Prairie and Brandon there could hardly be found one conifer tree of any kind. To-day there will be found little clumps of them here and there, and within a period of years that will again be a forest through the natural process of reforestation, if fires are kept out of it. The companies that are cutting timber, whether for saw logs or pulp, are realizing the value of leaving seed trees. One of the difficulties under the old methods of cutting was, as has been described by several hon. members in the discussion to-night, that a whole area would be denuded of' trees; but now trees are being left to reforest the area. All this knowledge is being acquired; some of it comes through the various experimental stations which the dominion government carries on under this vote, and other information is obtained concerning the work done in other countries. The important thing is to drive home to the public of Canada the vast importance of sound conservation policies and sound protection in regard to our forest work. The ravages from forest fires, for instance, are being reduced I think each year. Why? Because our people are more careful than they were when they go into the woods. They have learned that lesson; we must teach it to all.
Ravages by insects and parasites are also being studied. Reference has been made tonight to the ravage of the spruce trees in New Brunswick by a parasite called the spruce

Supply-Resources-Forests
bud worm, and its ravages have been very considerable in the Gaspe district in Quebec. There has been discovered in Europe a parasite that destroys the spruce bud worm. These parasites have been introduced into Canada and are being propagated by the entomological branch of the Department of Agriculture in a laboratory at Belleville. As they are propagated they are turned loose in these infested forest areas, and they do their work of destroying the spruce bud worm. All these matters are constantly under review and study, and I believe we are making substantial progress, but the important thing, I repeat, is to bring home to public opinion in this country the part which the individual citizen can play in this great work of conservation.

I think the minister is quite right in what he says in regard to conservation, but I would not like this discussion to be based upon the hypothesis that we are denuding the forests of Canada, if we are not actually doing it. After all, this is a matter of local concern because the provinces have charge of the forests, and in Nova Scotia this has been a vital question for many years. We have found that fire was a great hazard, that careless logging was a great hazard; but cutting is not the greatest hazard in our part of the country.
I was glad to hear the leader of the opposition say that it was advisable for the farmer to have two markets for his pulpwood. For a time in Nova Scotia the export of pulpwood was prohibited by statute except under licence by the attorney general. But the statute was not proclaimed. The export market is the market that protects the farmer who has pulpwood to sell.
I have heard that in Ontario, for instance, the annual cut does not exceed the wastage. If that is true, we should approach this conservation argument along a little different line. If we are denuding the forests of this country, it is a serious matter. If we are denuding our forests, it might be advisable not to ship so much lumber out of this country, and at the present time we are increasing our shipments of lumber. I think the federal government should be able to say when we reach the danger point with regard to the exporting or cutting of timber in Canada, and until we can do that, we cannot talk intelligently about denuding the forests of Canada.

I am particularly interested in the question of reforestation because the county of Simcoe from which I come was one of the first counties in Ontario, if not the first, which started reforestation. There we have a large area of land on which formerly
grew very fine forest pine. Here the county of Simcoe started a reforestation system, and when Mr. Drury, who was a citizen of our county, became premier of Ontario, he added his weight to the policy of reforestation in our province. There was an example, as has been suggested to-night, of how once you create public opinion in favour of a thing, it spreads throughout the country. If each of the provinces makes an effort to do its part, it will not be necessary for the federal government to do anything except assist in stimulating that public opinion, and continue its work in forest protection studies, and the operation of forest experimental stations.
As I said, in our county we have a large reforestation area, and now there are several farmers throughout the county who have land that is not fit for cultivation who have gradually been getting small trees from this reforestation plant and planting them themselves, so that to-day as one goes through the county one will see here and there several acres of spruce or pine which has been planted in the last fifteen or twenty years. The planting has gradually grown, and if other counties would do the same and have their own reforestation plants, we would soon have a great development along that line. I wish to add my voice, Mr. Chairman, to what has been said in regard to the importance of stimulating public opinion in this matter.
May I ask what is the cost per square mile of planting those trees?
I could not say offhand, but I can obtain the information for the hon. gentleman.
Thank you; I shall be very glad to have it.

I think the Minister of Lands and Forests in Ontario is to be commended for his policy. When a timber limit is let and the contractor starts his work, he is not allowed simply to take the valuable timber out, but he must take all the timber. I think the Minister of Lands and Forests is to be commended for removing the fire hazard by insisting on the cleaning up of the slash and the brush after a man has taken out valuable timber.

I have in mind what is unquestionably an historic site. Out at Watson's Corners, in the county of Lanark, Ontario, is a very old library site; if my memory serves me correctly, it is the second oldest library site in Ontario. After the settlement of Lanark county in 1820, Lord Dalhousie, who was a patron of the settlement, established at Watson's Corners a library and gave it a great many books. The original library building has disappeared, but many of the old books remain, in an old building within a quarter of a mile of the site of the original library. In my opinion that site should be marked in some way. The foundation remains, but there is nothing to identify it except a rude sign, which people living in the locality have placed there, stating that it is the site of the original library started about 1820 by Lord Dalhousie. If appropriations are made for marking sites, this is one which, on account of its historic connection with the inauguration of libraries and the dissemination of learning in this province, should be marked.

I might say that the historic sites which are marked are those selected by the historic sites and monuments board, and the department has nothing to do with the matter beyond providing the money to mark such sites as the board selects.
It may approve it.

The chairman, I know, is General E. A. Cruikshank of Ottawa, representing eastern Ontario and western Canada; the members are Mr. James H. Coyne, of St. Thomas, Ontario; Mr. Benjamin Suite, of Ottawa, representing Quebec and western

The present board is composed of:	General Cruikahank, chairman;

The late Senator Andrew Haydon, in his book, the Settlement of Bathurst, refers to it. Some of my own ancestral family settled around there about the year 1820, and some of them were on the library board shortly after that time. Does the department make a contribution to the marking of sites of that kind, and, if so, could it not write to the historic sites board suggesting that this site be so marked?

I have no objection to bringing to the notice of the board the remarks of the hon. member. But the selection of the site in each case rests with the board, and then the government provides the money to have the site properly marked.

With reference to this board, is it necessary for historical associations throughout the country-I am thinking of the Niagara peninsula in particular- to make representations to the board in order to have money expended in their areas, or does the minister appropriate this money to different sections of, for instance, the province of Ontario?

This item shows an increase of $114,982. Would the minister explain how this increase arises? Is it through the establishment of new parks, or more intensive development of existing parks, or partly one and partly the other? How does it arise?

Hon. members who were
here a year ago will recall that in the special supplementary estimates we had an appropriation for the establishment of parks in Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island. This increase is due to the vote being placed in the main estimates this year for those two parks.	.

Last year when parks were being discussed the minister in reply to the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) said that it was the intention of the department to have a resurvey of the sites in New Brunswick this year. He went on to say: "I hope to be able to come to parliament at the next session and make a definite recommendation as to a site in New Brunswick, and ask parliament for a vote to initiate the creation of a park in that province." I would ask the minister if there is to be a resurvey of areas in New Brunswick, and what the situation is at the present time with reference to the establishment of a park there. The people of New Brunswick are, I think, getting tired of the delay. They hardly know where to place the blame, whether on the federal department or on the local government. Last year
the premier of the province I think rather intimated that the delay was due to the federal department. These parks, I understand, are of great value for tourists. We are spending millions in the province for the construction of hard-surfaced roads, and the people of that province would like to see some start made on this national park, in order that we may be able to take advantage of the tourist traffic which is rapidly increasing, and I am sure will increase still more if a park is established somewhere in New Brunswick.

An examination was made by park officials of several sites in the province of New Brunswick during the past summer and autumn, and they gave a great deal of time and care to the matter. Those sites are at present under consideration by the provincial government. As my hon. friend is doubtless aware, the provincial government in each case has to supply the area which is finally settled upon as the park. Once the site is conveyed free of charge to the federal authorities, the responsibility is on the federal government to develop it. In connection with Cape Breton, for instance, I shall have some legislation before the house a little later making some changes in the boundary of that park. The provincial government found that it was going to cost a good deal to repossess some of the land which the Nova Scotia government had intended to convey to us. In the older settled provinces that is a problem. If the provincial governments of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick set aside a considerable area as a park, they have to give us a clear title to that area.
The boundaries were defined in the statute last year.

Yes; that is why I have to come back this session and ask for some changes in the definition of the boundaries. I have no doubt the New Brunswick government is examining the whole question carefully because the matter of cost is involved. There are several factors; there is cost and the suitability of the site for park purposes. As I said, the park officials have made a thorough survey of and an inquiry into the matter in New Brunswick. Half a dozen sites were suggested, but it really narrows down to three or four and they are now under consideration by the government of New Brunswick. Probably they will come back and say:	We prefer you to take this site
because we can secure title at less cost than for another site. Then it becomes a matter of negotiation between the two governments.

I should like the minister to tell us why the national park in New Brunswick should be in the seat of the hon. member for Royal, the only Tory seat in the maritime provinces.

I indicated to the minister last year how strong I thought the claims of New Brunswick were to a park. There is a park in Nova Scotia and one in Prince Edward Island, which is a very small area. As most tourists to get to Nova Scotia, that is, those who do not go there by sea, have to pass through New Brunswick, and having regard to the fact that I was born in New Brunswick, the minister would naturally desire to place a park there. There is the further consideration that we were so poor during the time we were in office that we could not afford to start a park in New Brunswick. Had we been able to do so we should have done it, to be perfectly frank-
Call it Bennett park.

I had not thought of that. If the hon. member for Huron North (Mr. Deachman) were here, he would say that I have done enough harm to this country without having a park named after me. But it seems to me the time has come when a park should be established in New Brunswick. In view of the establishment of a park in Cape Breton and one on Prince Edward Island, putting this off will only make the difficulty greater. I think the minister knows from experience that that is so. As I understand the matter, however, the government here must determine which of several sites they will accept, if several are offered by the provincial government, which may say: We are prepared to supply title for a park at either so-and-so or so-and-so, and then this government must say whether it will accept that site for a park. For instance, in Nova Scotia they offered a site in Cape Breton and the federal government accepted it. Prince Edward Island, not to be outdone by Nova Scotia, provided a small area, and the government accepted it. In New Brunswick there are three areas that I know were discussed; one is in one of the old counties-it is not a Tory county either, which is very much to be regretted in the interests of the nation as a whole and of my hon. friend in particular- there is one in the county of Charlotte and one in the county of Albert. Another area has also been suggested. If I have some prejudice in favour of the county in which I was born, the minister will understand my 
feelings. I urge the desirability of some action being taken at an early date, because the longer the matter is allowed to go on the more difficult it is going to be for the minister. I hope we shall be able to find some money for it. All I can say to my hon. friend is that I am going to do my best.

After all, however, we must carry on the work of the department according to the means we have at our disposal. I have no doubt that in due time Garibaldi park may be considered, but I would ask the hon. member not to press it too closely at the present time.

I believe the parks branch
is losing a great amount of revenue due to the

fact that the Big Bend highway is not yet completed. I am quite sure that when it is completed American tourists will come up to Vancouver, and from there go through to Banff. I should like to know the present position with regard to the uncompleted portion of the Big Ben highway which, as the minister is aware, is the only uncompleted portion of the trans-Canada highway in western Canada, and for that reason also is very important.

That matter will be discussed under another vote. I may say, however, that there is an appropriation-I have forgotten just how much-to carry on the work on that section of the trans-Canada highway. It is scarcely necessary to remind the hon. member that the federal government is building that section of the highway to relieve the province of British Columbia of expenditures in connection with it. That was done because road building in British Columbia is a costly affair, owing to the rugged nature of the country. Possibly after that road is completed and we complete some other work, we might be in a position to consider claims with respect to Garibaldi park.

When will the Big Bend
link be completed?
1939, I think.
How many miles are there?

There is work to be done between Golden and Donald this year. The road from Donald to the Canoe river, including a bridge across the Canoe river, is practically completed. A substantial part of the road between the Canoe river and Revelstoke is completed, and balance of the work will be under way this year. There is some work to be done between Golden and Donald.

Does the minister know
how many miles?
I cannot give that information at the moment, but I shall have it when the vote is before the committee.
Will the minister indicate how much of the vote is to be spent in each of the provinces?
I am sorry we have not the vote set up in a manner which will give that information readily. If I had a lightning calculator here, I could do it.
Can the minister procure it?

Yes; we can procure almost anything.
